objective.x: To introspect on our waste producing habits/lifestyle.
To localize the issue, and discuss our direct relation with it; which will later help when we discuss individual ways of reducing waste.
MATERIALS – Games/Quiz, discussions, worksheets, film screening
The session will begin with a quick recap of the last session with a rapid-fire quiz.

Students will be divided into two teams, one will ask questions and the other will answer. So it will be a rapid fire quiz amongst them. They will be given 5 minutes to prepare a total of 15 short answer/one word questions.
Next a discussion will be held with the students to discuss about one’s own waste producing habits, which will help recognize our individual impact on the issue of waste production and management
Firstly, the students will be asked to think of and tell of our actions that lead to production of waste, after jotting their observations down.

Through a short film screening of the film ‘Wasted’, students can trace the journey of our collective waste, which will help them realize, in detail, the impact of the waste that each and every individual in our city produces, and will also act as the base of the next session which will be a walk to one of the landfills in Delhi.
Post the screening, a quiz (worksheet attached) based on it will be conducted, to ascertain student’s increased understanding of waste and its lifecycle. (10 min)

discussion.x: Discussions may be led on how lifestyle changes have led to increased waste production
Students may be asked to compare what they currently do which, maybe their grandparents would not have done in their youth, which has created a lot of waste.
Urban India (about 377 million people) generates 62 million tonnes of municipal solid
waste each year, of this about 43 million tonnes (70%) is collected and 11.9 million tonnes (20%) is treated. About 31 million tonnes (50%) is dumped in landfill sites.
With changing consumption patterns and rapid economic growth it is estimated that urban
municipal solid waste generation will increase to 165 million tonnes in 2030
MSW typically contains 51% organic waste, 17% recyclables, 11% hazardous and 21%

inert waste. However, about 40% of all MSW is not collected at all and hence lies littered in the city/town and finds its way to nearby drains and water bodies, causing choking as well as pollution of surface water. Unsegregated waste collection and transportation leads to dumping in the open, which generates leachate and gaseous emissions besides causing nuisance in the surrounding environment. Leachate contaminates the groundwater as well as surface water in the vicinity and gaseous emissions contribute to global warming.
